Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
Nothing good can happen to me anymore
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger items are not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of police violence. Snake-related cues and fire/flames do not plausibly connect to police violence unless there were unusual event details, and no other selected items suggest such a context. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain for the same trauma.

Within Memory, 'Vivid Memory' and 'Memory Gaps' can coexist in PTSD, but 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with a severe PTSD presentation and with the memory disturbance pattern implied by the other memory items. It suggests unusually easy narrative access despite simultaneously endorsing vivid re-experiencing and amnestic gaps, which is internally inconsistent here.

Fire/flames is hard to reconcile as a trauma trigger for police violence in the absence of any corroborating memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to fire; 'Police' as an authority trigger fits, but 'fire/flames' appears trauma-incongruent for this profile.

issues.item: Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
issues.explanation: The Memory node contains a direct internal contradiction: endorsing very clear/detailed memories, irretrievable gaps, and very easy verbal access all together is not clinically coherent as stated. Vivid memory can coexist with some gaps, but pairing both with 'I can talk about what happened very easily' strongly conflicts with a severe PTSD profile and with the fragmented/distressing memory pattern implied by the other memory items.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked trauma-memory disruption indicated by both severe memory gaps and fragmented, disconnected recollections. Those memory items imply impaired coherent access to the trauma narrative, making very easy verbal access hard to reconcile clinically in the same profile.

vignette:
Meera knew the texture before she knew what it was. A rough, industrial-grade carpet fiber beneath her cheek. The smell of floor polish and stale coffee. She was seventy-three years old, an interior designer who had spent four decades specifying fabrics and finishes, and now her own body had become a museum of sensations she could not name. The event itself—the police raid on her son’s home three years ago—arrived in her mind as a series of broken snapshots: the door splintering inward, a voice shouting, then the pressure of a knee between her shoulder blades. She could not remember how she had gotten from the doorway to the floor. There were minutes, perhaps whole sequences, that simply did not exist. When she tried to tell her daughter what happened, the words collapsed. She knew what she had seen—the uniforms, the batons, the way her son’s hands were cuffed behind his back—but language failed her, and she would sit in her kitchen, mouth open, unable to finish a single sentence. Once she had concluded that her memory was broken and her body was a traitor, she began scanning the world for anything that might confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her — and each time she found something, it proved her right.

The uniforms followed her. A police cruiser at a red light, a security guard outside a bank, a military veteran in a baseball cap at the grocery store. Each sighting sent a current through her chest, and she would find herself gripping a shopping cart, breath shallow, heart hammering. She had come to believe that her body was no longer her ally. It reacted as though the danger were still happening, even when she was perfectly safe—standing in the produce aisle, or folding laundry in her own living room. Because she believed her body would betray her at any moment, she began scanning her environment for anything that might set it off — a loud noise, a sudden movement, a door slamming nearby — and each time she found one, it confirmed she had been right to worry. That belief, that her body was a traitor, made every small upset feel catastrophic—a dropped glass, a forgotten appointment, a slightly raised voice from a neighbor now registered as a potential threat because she had concluded that nothing was safe anymore. That belief, that her body was a traitor, made every small upset feel catastrophic. A dropped glass, a forgotten appointment, a slightly raised voice from a neighbor: each one confirmed that she could not handle even the gentlest pressure from the world. Nothing good could happen anymore. She was certain of it. What was the point of selecting throw pillows for a client’s condo when the world could break down your door at any moment?

The texture came back most often at night. A rough blanket against her cheek, the corduroy of her armchair, the grain of a wooden headboard. Any of these could send her spiraling back to that carpet, that floor, that helplessness. And once the memory surfaced—fragmented, wordless, incomplete—her negative appraisals sharpened. See, her mind would whisper, you cannot even remember what happened. You are falling apart. You will never be safe. Her conviction that she would never be safe meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every unexpected sound, every car door slamming, every glance from a stranger became a potential signal that the next raid was beginning. This loop tightened over months. She stopped taking new clients. She avoided the side of town where her son still lived. She stopped driving past police stations, then stopped driving altogether. Her daughter began doing the grocery shopping. Meera stayed home, arranging and rearranging the cushions on her sofa, trying to make the world feel soft again.

What finally brought her to seek help was a single moment: a police officer knocked on her door to ask about a lost dog in the neighborhood. Meera opened the door, saw the uniform, and vomited onto the welcome mat. She stood there, shaking, as the officer backed away apologizing. That night, she called a clinic. She was most afraid that nothing would change, that her body would remain a stranger to her, that the gaps in her memory would never fill. But she was also, quietly, hoping that someone could help her find the words.
